thread.title: Apple To Enter A Slow Growth Period? Think Again - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: D.M. Martins Research
title: Apple To Enter A Slow Growth Period? Think Again - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
If Apple ( AAPL ) is supposed to enter a period of slow growth, as a few experts have recently suggested , somebody needs to let the company's management team know first.
Seemingly fearless of a slowdown in its robust growth pace, or perhaps proactively attempting to avoid one, Apple has recently reiterated its plans to hire thousands of workers in the United States over the next five years - 5,000 in the newly-announced Austin, Texas, campus alone.
Credit: Business Insider
What it is Back in January of this year and a few weeks after the signing of the December 2017 tax reform into law, the Cupertino company unveiled its plan to boost capital investments, increase spending with suppliers and manufacturers, and promote job creation in the United States. Regarding the latter, management's idea was to add 20,000 employees to the company's payroll by 2023 - a sizable headcount increase of nearly 25% from 4Q17 levels. It's now known that at least one-fourth of this total will be housed in the new North Austin campus, which is expected to cost Apple $1 billion to build.
I believe this Thursday's announcement of the new campus location is meaningful not only because of the magnitude of the numbers. I find it particularly interesting that the reiteration of Apple's growth plan happens precisely when (1) talks of a struggling 2018 iPhone lineup continue to surface , (2) the trade war between the U.S. and China threatens to cause disruption to Apple's supply chain and, possibly, result in higher production costs, and (3) Apple's stock has pulled back 25% from its previous peak for the first time since May 2016 .
Source: company's press release
What it means financially Assuming that Apple has not changed much of its original plans , the 5,000 new jobs to be created in Texas are likely to be in technical customer support functions. According to Glassdoor , an Apple technical support agent in the U.S. makes approximately $38,000 per year in salaries. The average might perhaps approach $45,000 once wage inflation, job oversupply and the need for middle-management personnel are taken into account.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics estimates that only about two-thirds of employee compensation takes the form of salaries (the remaining one-third are benefits), pushing the total compensation cost of each new North Austin employee added to the payroll to about $67,500 - excluding recruiting costs that should further beef up SG&A. Add payroll taxes of up to 10% that include Social Security, Medicare and state unemployment, and we are probably looking at a total additional cost of about $72,000 per head per year.
Simple math suggests, therefore, that the new Texas campus should cost the Cupertino company some $365 million in extra personnel expenses annually. While financial figures tend to be measured in the billions of dollars in the Apple world, this is not necessarily pocket change. In fiscal 2018, for example, Apple incurred $16.7 billion in SG&A expenses. The extra $365 million alone would represent a decrease of nearly 20 bps in total company op margin in future years, per my estimates.
Source: DM Martins Research estimates
Of course, this is only part of the story. The 5,000 new employees in North Austin account for only one fourth of the total estimated headcount increase by 2023. The other 15,000 positions could in fact be associated with higher-income professionals in fields like "advanced design, engineering and research," as described by the company in January - a few dozen medical doctors, for example, have been reportedly hired to assist with Apple's health tech initiatives recently. A total, blended average cost per new employee of $100,000 is certainly not out of question, in my opinion.
Should this be the case, I estimate that Apple's job creation efforts in the U.S. should produce $2 billion in extra personnel expenses alone and might impact Apple's fiscal 2023 EPS negatively by roughly 50 cents (see chart above) - assuming, for simplicity, a stable tax rate and a share count that drops by about 6% per year. At a P/E multiple of 16x that's consistent with the stock's average of the past 12 months (see below), the extra SG&A cost in the U.S. would represent about $8 in share price headwind.
AAPL PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts Conclusion AAPL bears might look at the facts and figures above and conclude that the company's inflated cost base will exert bottom-line pressures that might not be justified by the company's growth profile. Bulls, myself included, probably believe instead that the aggressive growth plans are indicative of management's confidence in Apple's performance over the next several years. They further reinforce my convictions that revenues and earnings are likely to continue marching forward, driven increasingly more by a services portfolio that should surpass $12 billion in quarterly revenues by fiscal 2020.
More so now, following the stock's sharp pullback, I remain an AAPL bull at current levels. Had I not been invested in this stock as much as I believe it to be prudent, I would consider now a good time to buy additional shares on recent price weakness.
